column2: As news of Ma Xinyi’s appointment reached Zhejiang, an important and intriguing report arrived from Jiangxi: the young rebel Hong Tianguifu had at last been captured. The campaign against the Taipings was drawing to a close, but formidable work remained before disorder could be put down. In the judgment of Prince Gong and Wenxiang, three rebellions still stood between the empire and lasting peace: the Taiping remnants who had fled south, the Nian bands disturbing the central provinces, and the Muslim rebellions devastating the western frontier. Fortunately, men of talent abounded in numbers surpassing earlier reigns. Prince Gong and Wenxiang decided to entrust the suppression of these three troubles to four men. The first was still Zeng Guofan. On the first day of the tenth month, as Zeng Guoquan retired in triumph and led the disbanded Hunan troops home, a confidential dispatch reached Jiangning: “Jiangning is now entirely pacified, and military operations there are concluded. Zeng Guofan shall select a portion of his forces and proceed to the Anhui–Hubei border to direct the suppression of the rebels. He must advance speedily and permit no delay.” These “rebels” were the Nian.

The Nian had originally made northern Anhui their base. Under Prince Sengge Rinchen’s vigorous attacks, they had moved into Hubei and Henan. Though Zhang Luoxing was dead, his nephew Zhang Zongyu was no weak successor. Lai Wenguang, formerly one of Chen Yucheng’s commanders, had also returned from Guanzhong. With the Heavenly Capital fallen, he was a man without a home; naturally he joined the Nian, greatly increasing their strength and boldness. The court knew that the prince’s cavalry tactics—pursuing and driving the Nian from place to place—were unsound. Once his troops exhausted themselves, a rebel counterattack must bring disaster. Yet his exalted position made him extremely difficult to handle. Even the Western Empress Dowager had to show him special indulgence. Offer strategic instructions, and he could invoke the maxim that a commander in the field need not obey every order of his sovereign. Press him a little, and he might take offense and act entirely on his own. It would be better, for public and private reasons alike, to find a way for him to relinquish his command and return to enjoy life in Beijing. Only Zeng Guofan could replace him in directing operations across several provinces. His prestige was sufficient, and his practice of “seeking security first and flexibility afterward”—meeting movement with stillness, advancing steadily from firm positions—would correct the prince’s mistakes. For the financing of the campaign, the court had thought of another indispensable man.

That man was Li Hongzhang. An edict appointed him to act in Zeng’s place as Governor-General of Liangjiang, while Wu Tang, Director-General of Grain Transport and a benefactor of Empress Dowager Cixi, was transferred to act as Governor of Jiangsu. The decree did not expressly state that Li would bear full responsibility for the rear supply bureau supporting Zeng on the Anhui–Hubei frontier, but the intention was plain. First, Zeng and Li were teacher and pupil; it was only proper that “when there is work to be done, the disciple undertakes the labor.” Second, Zeng had raised funds when Li commanded in the field; now their roles should be reversed. Third, Liangjiang was the richest region and a principal source of military revenue, so whoever governed it was bound to provide funds. Viewed in terms of the general situation, the arrangement was sound. It merely disadvantaged Zeng and benefited Li and Wu—but not every consideration could be accommodated.

Another man selected was Yang Yuebin, a naval commander whose fame equaled Peng Yulin’s. His original name was Yang Zaifu. Since the first character of the Tongzhi Emperor’s generation in the imperial genealogy was Zai, however, the name risked offending the naming taboo, and he changed it to Yuebin. Before Jiangning fell he had already been appointed Governor-General of Shaanxi and Gansu, with the intention of entrusting him with the suppression of the Muslim rebellion. Such rebellions had broken out not only there but in Yunnan and Xinjiang as well. Yunnan was approaching pacification, while Xinjiang’s troubles were gathering force. For the latter, the court placed its hopes in the newly created viscount Bao Chao. A warmly worded decree declared that without “a man of exceptional courage and strategy such as Bao Chao” it would be difficult to transform the military situation in Xinjiang. Zeng was therefore ordered to transmit instructions that, upon the expiry of Bao’s two-month leave to bury his parent, he should “depart immediately from Sichuan, pass beyond the frontier, and suppress the Muslim rebellion.” Knowing Bao’s love of renown, Prince Gong and Wenxiang flattered him by comparing him with Yang Yuchun, the celebrated general of the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns. “In former campaigns in the Muslim territories, Yang Yuchun, himself a native of Sichuan, won frontier victories whose glory shone upon the military banners. Bao Chao must lead his forces to pacify the western marches, carrying his fame ten thousand li and matching the splendor of his predecessor. Loyal and brave by nature, he will surely obey upon receiving this decree and fulfill the court’s trust.” The language was most earnest. By requiring Zeng to transmit it, the court also hinted that he should help urge Bao forward. Zeng, however, had long resolved that the Hunan Army should withdraw prudently at the height of its success. Bao was a favorite commander whom he particularly wished to protect. He simply conveyed the edict in the usual way and offered no encouragement to depart.

The other man in whom the court placed great hopes was Zuo. As Governor-General of Fujian and Zhejiang, he was naturally responsible for suppressing the two large forces of Li Shixian and Wang Haiyang, defeated by Bao at Ruijin in Jiangxi and driven into Fujian. Zuo was not a man to shrink from trouble. He regarded the duty as his by right and could not honorably refuse. Yet a succession of court decisions made him angry, anxious, and deeply resentful. His first disappointment was Ma Xinyi’s appointment to Zhejiang. Jiang Yili had been passed over, which meant that Zuo had lost control of the province. Next came Li’s transfer to act as Governor-General of Liangjiang, placing him above Zuo in standing and precedence—a most unpleasant thought. Then Yang Yuebin, still in Jiangxi, was ordered to proceed promptly to his post in Shaanxi and Gansu. Zhejiang was required to contribute a hundred thousand taels a month toward his military expenses and first to raise eighty thousand for his army’s departure. Zuo’s temper flared. Every day, when receiving his staff, he roundly abused Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang, and Guo Songtao. After several days his anger abated a little. Since he would not resign and return to farming, he must undertake something substantial and impressive. He was confident of his military ability; the difficulty was an ever-shrinking revenue base. Before Ma arrived, he needed a resourceful man to help arrange matters properly.

That man could only be Hu. “Mr Xueyan,” Zuo said, “they have squeezed me until I have nowhere to turn. Where do you think I can raise funds? It is difficult everywhere.” Together they went through the fifteen provinces one by one. Leaving aside the poor provinces, every wealthy source of revenue had already been claimed. Jiangsu and Anhui lay within Liangjiang, where Zeng and his pupil Li were deeply entrenched. Shen Baozhen’s treatment of the Hunan Army in Jiangxi was warning enough. Shandong and Shanxi supplied the capital, and their governors, Yan Jingming and Shen Guifen, were upright, shrewd, and difficult men to deal with. Hubei consumed Sichuan salt, collecting substantial likin revenue through an office at Shashi. But Guanwen was the only bannerman among the governors and governors-general; right or wrong, he enjoyed the court’s protection, and gaining access there would be hard. As for prosperous Sichuan, Luo Bingzhang governed it. Remembering their old relationship as patron and secretary, Zuo could hardly bring himself to play out a “seizure of Chengdu.” “Fujian is desperately poor. The only places left to me are your province and Guangdong. Guangdong withholds the contributions due to me. That hateful Guo Yunxian recognizes no one but Zeng Disheng and Li Shaoquan! I cannot forget it.” Zuo paused. “As for Ma Gushan, I hear he is reasonable enough. But Zeng recommended him, and he passed the examinations in the same year as Li. He may not be willing to help me. Mr Xueyan, what am I to do?”

Hu remained silent. His position was difficult. He must repay Zuo’s recognition and favor, yet Zhejiang was his home province. He could not devise schemes for Zuo that would earn the curses of its people. Hu usually spoke decisively and accepted even the greatest difficulties without hesitation; such a prolonged silence was almost unprecedented. Mildly surprised, Zuo pressed him for an explanation. “To be frank, my lord, I am in a difficult position. Zhejiang is now the only province you can draw upon, so naturally your supplies and pay must come from it. Raise too little, and it will not suffice; raise too much, and the people suffer. Everyone will say it was my idea. Among my own countrymen, that would be an uncomfortable position. If you continued to act as Governor of Zhejiang, I could still suggest ways to balance one source against another and adapt to circumstances, taking both interests into account. But Governor Ma is coming. I am only a probationary circuit intendant assigned to Jiangxi, whom you had transferred here for service. Once you leave Zhejiang, I shall have no right to concern myself with its affairs. I must even hand over my post at the Reconstruction Bureau, let alone anything else.”

Zuo nodded throughout. When Hu finished, he gestured for patience. “I understand all the circumstances you have described. We must discuss them carefully. Through every change, one principle remains: you must continue to help me. How you are to help we shall consider presently. First, let us deal with your difficulty. As you say, Zhejiang is my only base, and Zhejiang must provide my army’s funds. Moreover, there must be a fixed sum, remitted each month on a fixed date, not one day late. Mr Xueyan, in everything we first establish what is reasonable, then appeal to personal feeling. If both reason and feeling support us and we still cannot prevail, I naturally have methods of my own.” Hu did not know what the last words implied. Keeping to the immediate issue, he asked, “What sum do you intend to fix, my lord?” “What would you suggest?” Zuo lowered his voice. “Between ourselves, I shall tell you the truth. I actually have eighteen thousand men, but funding must allow a margin. We should calculate for twenty-three thousand.” Hu reckoned rapidly. A soldier’s monthly pay, grain, weapons, ammunition, horse fodder, and miscellaneous needs—tents, cooking pots, bowls, and the rest—averaged five taels. Twenty-three thousand men meant a hundred and fifteen thousand taels. Add the commander’s own expenses, the salaries and board of secretaries and commissioned officials, and the costs of hospitality, and no less than a hundred and fifty thousand taels a month would do.

For Zhejiang to bear that enormous sum alone was too much. Hu therefore spoke tactfully. “Fujian and Zhejiang are one family. Over the years, Fujian has contributed at least three million taels toward Zhejiang’s military expenses. Now that Fujian has trouble, we should naturally help. Besides, the troops you command are Zhejiang troops; Zhejiang ought to pay them. But you understand the province’s condition better than anyone. If we could determine our income by our expenditure, matters would be easier.” The usual maxim was to determine expenditure by income; Hu had reversed it, which was something new. Stroking his drooping mustache, Zuo asked with a smile, “What do you mean by determining income by expenditure? I should like to hear.” “Suppose there is a bowl of soup. One man takes a ladleful, another takes a ladleful; very little reaches anyone’s mouth—” “Ah!” Zuo interrupted. “I understand. I had the same thought. First, we absolutely cannot agree to the contribution for Shaanxi and Gansu. Second, Guangdong’s contribution to Zhejiang exists only in name. I shall petition to have it discontinued.” At this his eyes moved from side to side, and a slow, exceedingly secretive smile spread over his face.

There was much behind that smile. Hu felt he must understand it and deliberately probed. “Guangdong’s contribution is a picture of a cake. Though it cannot feed us, it is something to look at.” “No. By asking for its cancellation, I shall show the court that it is only a painted cake. Mr Xueyan—” Zuo suddenly grew excited. “Watch this old man’s methods! I shall turn the painted cake into a great thick barley cake, enough to fill our bellies. Do you believe me?” “Of course. Will you need me as an assistant in this conjuring trick?” “Naturally! Without you I could never perform this trick of producing a cake from bare ground—and sawing a living man in two besides.” Though meant as a joke, the last words were jarring. Half in jest, Hu asked, “Whom do you mean to saw in two, my lord?” “Whom?” Zuo’s smile had grown fierce. “My own in-law.” Hu was appalled. He had long known that Zuo bore a grievance against Guo Songtao, one that time had deepened rather than eased. But how had it reached the point of such language? For a moment he stood speechless. Zuo too ceased smiling. His face grew serious, his eyes wide, his mouth firmly closed; yet his gaze flickered and his lips moved, as though powerful waves were passing through his mind. Hu listened with even closer attention to hear how this “sawing a living man in two” was to be done.

“Xueyan!” For the first time Zuo dropped the formal address and used his courtesy name, treating him as an intimate friend. “I know you have not read many books. But understanding the world is itself learning, and in that respect I admire you.” “You are too kind.” Hu was a little uneasy but remained frank. “If you have something to say, please give me your instructions. Such a tall hat of praise is rather too much for me.” “Why should I need flattery between us? What I mean is that you understand half of my character and conduct. The other half you not only fail to understand, but may strongly disapprove of. That is because you have read too little. If you had studied more, you would understand that other half as well, and see that I have no choice: circumstances compel it.” So that was what he meant. Hu felt almost overwhelmed by the confidence shown him. “My lord, if you speak to me of ‘the Way of Great Learning lies in manifesting luminous virtue,’ I shall understand nothing.” “I shall speak of history, not the Classics. First, tell me what these two sayings mean: ‘For a greater righteousness, sacrifice even one’s kin,’ and ‘For public duty, forget private interests.’”

Hu had no answer, nor felt one was needed. He replied honestly, “Please do not examine me, my lord. Begin with those sayings and tell me your plans.” “I am not examining you. My point is that ordinary people may condemn my actions bitterly. Yet though I fail my kin, I do not fail what is right; though I may be ashamed in private relationships, I have nothing to blush for in public duty. Common opinion cannot understand this. Only a learned man will say in his heart: ‘Zuo is a hero born for his age. He could do no otherwise.’” The speech was rather bookish, but Hu understood it well enough and grasped its implication: Zuo meant to deal Guo Songtao a severe blow. What he could not see was what blow lay within Zuo’s power. His question was answered at once. Zuo rose, sat at his desk, took a brush, and spread out paper. He rapidly drew a map, adding place-names among the curved lines and dots. Hu recognized the Fujian–Guangdong frontier. “Li Shixian is at Zhangzhou, which fell on the fourteenth day of the ninth month. Brigade Commander Lukui was killed in action; Circuit Intendant Xu Xiaofeng of Tingzhou, Zhangzhou, and Longyan died at his post. Li has probably more than eight thousand men and must not be underestimated.” Pointing to the triangle formed by Changting, Liancheng, and Shanghang, Zuo continued, “Wang Haiyang is here. In my judgment he is fiercer than Li. Still, there is no cause for alarm about putting these rebels down. Xueyan, you must have learned a little strategy in recent years. Where do you think Li and Wang can escape?”

For a moment Hu seemed stumped. He studied the map closely before answering. “They came from Jiangxi in the west. To the east lies the sea, a long way off—and without ships they could not put to sea anyway. In the north, your troops are pressing down. Ah!” Understanding came suddenly, and he spoke with confidence. “Their only way out is south into Guangdong. Jiaying Prefecture will bear the first attack.” Zuo nodded deeply, stroking his mustache with a smile. “Exactly. Jiaying will bear the first attack. Then we shall no longer be feeding ourselves on painted cakes.” There was a hidden meaning in his words. He did not continue, and Hu dared not ask, fearing that a mistaken guess might lead him into a grave indiscretion. Zuo, however, had no such reservations. He truly regarded Hu as a confidant fit to hear the deepest secrets. “Guo Yunxian has always feared that Zeng Disheng would drive the rebels into Guangdong. He never imagined it would be his own in-law who did so. When that happens, Xueyan, the situation will be entirely different.” Hu shuddered involuntarily. Zuo’s methods seemed altogether too ruthless. He had guessed this very thing, certainly; but a conjecture was one matter, and hearing it confirmed in the man’s own words was another.

“Xueyan, tell me what the situation will be then.” “Yes.” Hu considered. “The court will naturally turn to your prestige and ability, appoint you imperial commissioner, and place military affairs in Fujian, Zhejiang, and Guangdong under your authority. Governor Guo—” He stopped. His meaning was clear: under Zuo’s handling, Guo would suffer severely. “Precisely. Circumstances must lead to that. Then, Xueyan, I shall no longer burden Zhejiang. Guo Yunxian will have to raise funds obediently for me. Unless—” Zuo pondered for a long while. “There is no certainty. Guo is foolish and obstinate. He may still refuse to see reason.” “And if he does, my lord, what will you do?”
